title: He gave his head, not his faith
hookLine: of his father he writes that he gave his head but not his faith (Bachitar Natak 5)

lines: A SON WHOSE FATHER WAS EXECUTED.
A FEW LINES, EVERY WORD CHOSEN.
cards: At a funeral, the hardest speech belongs to the child. Everyone is waiting to hear what the son or daughter will say: which memory, which word, which part of the life to hold up.

Guru Gobind Singh lost his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, to an execution in Delhi. When he came to tell his own life in verse, in Bachitar Natak, he gave his father a few lines. They are short, and every word is chosen.

teach.b: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. He protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread, and did a great deed in this dark age. For the sake of the holy, he gave his head, and did not cry out.
For the sake of dharma, he did this deed: he gave his head, but not his faith. Look at who the first line protects. Those were the signs of another community's worship, not his own.
The son remembers his father dying for someone else's right to pray.
Then the pair at the center: he gave his head, sis dia, but not his sirar. Sirar is a word Sikhs gloss as his faith, his resolve, the inner thing that can't be handed over. The body could be taken.
That couldn't. The Guru goes on: he writes that his father would not do tricks to save himself.
The people of God, he says in paraphrase, are ashamed to perform a juggler's wonders. No miracle show for an emperor, just a man who wouldn't move.
And then an image: he broke the clay pot of his body on the head of the king of Delhi, and went to the Lord's own place. A clay pot, smashed.
Some readers hear in it that the death landed on the one who ordered it, and that the father walked on, unbroken, into God's presence.
For a son, this is grief turned into witness. He doesn't dwell on the blade; he tells you what his father kept.
Days ago, telling the ninth Guru's stand for freedom of conscience, this path borrowed one of these lines in passing. Today the whole passage gets its own hearing, in his son's voice.

how: Sikhs recall these lines from Bachitar Natak when they remember the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and sis dia par sirar na dia is quoted in katha and kirtan.

games.q: what does “he gave his head” mean?
o: he bowed his head in surrender to the emperor
he died for others' faith, keeping his own
he gave up his title to save his own family

games.q: a son's lines for his father: tap the pairs.
p: his body, broken on the king's head

s: the lines say Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending his own community's signs
they say he protected their mark and their thread, the signs of others' worship.
in his son's account, he refused to perform wonders to save himself
the people of God, the poem says, are ashamed to perform a juggler's tricks.
the son's lines dwell on the details of the execution
he tells what his father kept: he gave his head, but not his faith.

games.q: you're the son, writing your father's death into your life story. what do you hold up?
o: what he refused to give up, and for whom.
nothing; it's too painful to write.
games.why: Guru Gobind Singh writes that his father protected others' mark and thread, and gave his head but not his faith.

practice: Ask yourself, gently: what is one thing in me I wouldn't hand over? Not a possession but a principle: honesty with a child, fairness at work, standing up for someone else's right to be who they are.
Let it come into focus and see yourself holding it, no drama, just not moving; if you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: He gave his head. The tenth Guru's words for his father: he gave his head, but not his faith, for the right of others to worship their own way. Today's word.
